questions.question: What is polymorphism in Python, and how does duck typing support it?
questions.title: Python Polymorphism and Duck Typing
questions.direct_answer: Polymorphism means one operation can work with objects of different types. Python often achieves it through duck typing: code relies on the required behaviour or protocol instead of demanding a particular inheritance chain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand shared behaviour across different concrete types, not merely method overriding vocabulary.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying duck typing accepts any object; the object still has to provide the operations the code uses.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the small behavioural contract and show unrelated classes satisfying it.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Polymorphism gives one operation meaningful behaviour for different types.
Overriding lets subclasses provide their own implementation of a base method.
Duck typing depends on supported operations, not declared ancestry.
Unrelated classes can satisfy the same informal protocol.
The required behaviour must still be documented and tested.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Polymorphism means the same operation can be used with values of different concrete types, while each value provides behaviour appropriate to itself. Python has built-in examples such as `len()`, and user code can get polymorphism through overriding or through a shared protocol.

Duck typing is Python's common protocol-based form. A function does not need an object to inherit from one named base class; it needs the object to support the methods or attributes the function actually uses. The object's behaviour is the contract.

For example, an `EmailReport` and a `PdfReport` can be unrelated classes that both implement `render()`. A `publish(report)` function can call `report.render()` for either object. Adding another report type requires implementing that operation, not changing `publish`.

Duck typing is not the absence of a contract. Passing an object without `render` raises an error when that operation is reached. Type hints with `Protocol`, tests, or an abstract base class can make expectations more visible. I prefer the smallest clear interface so implementations remain replaceable without depending on unrelated details.

sections.title: Program to the operation the caller needs
sections.content:
A polymorphic caller stays stable while concrete behaviour varies. Instead of checking `if type is EmailReport` and selecting code manually, it sends the same request to each object. That moves type-specific knowledge into the type that owns it.

Inheritance provides one route: a base class names an operation and subclasses override it. Python's runtime does not require that family relationship for ordinary method calls, though. Attribute lookup simply tries to find the requested operation on the receiver. This structural quality is called duck typing.

The design works well when the expected protocol is focused. If a function needs only `render()`, requiring ten unrelated methods creates unnecessary coupling. If the failure must be detected before runtime, a `typing.Protocol` can describe the same structural contract for a static checker, while an ABC can create a nominal runtime family.

sections.title: Different types, one required operation
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[publish report] --> R[Call report.render]
  E[EmailReport] -->|provides render| R
  D[PdfReport] -->|provides render| R
  H[HtmlReport] -->|provides render| R
  R --> O[Renderable output]
```

questions.question: Does Python support method overloading and method overriding?
questions.title: Method Overloading vs Overriding in Python
questions.direct_answer: Python supports overriding through inheritance, but a class cannot keep several ordinary methods with the same name as signature-based overloads; the last definition replaces earlier ones. Optional arguments, dispatch tools, or type-hint overloads serve different needs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you distinguish runtime overriding from the signature-based overload selection found in languages such as Java.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing two methods with the same name and expecting Python to choose by argument count.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate runtime implementation, default-argument design, `singledispatchmethod`, and static-only `typing.overload`.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Overriding replaces inherited behaviour in a subclass.
Repeated same-name definitions in one class do not create runtime overloads.
The last ordinary definition bound to the name wins.
Default or keyword arguments often cover simple call variations.
`typing.overload` helps static checkers but supplies no runtime dispatch.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Python supports method overriding. A subclass defines a method with the same name as an inherited method, and normal method lookup finds the subclass version first. The overriding method can call `super()` when it wants to extend rather than fully replace the inherited behaviour.

Python does not provide Java-style runtime overloading merely by declaring several methods with the same name and different parameter lists. A class body is a namespace, so a later `def format(...)` assignment replaces the earlier value bound to `format`.

For example, one `format_message` method can accept an optional `prefix=None` and handle both call forms explicitly. For genuinely type-specific runtime dispatch, `functools.singledispatchmethod` is available, though simple APIs often remain clearer with different method names or one normalized input.

`typing.overload` has another purpose: it describes several accepted signatures to a static type checker, followed by one real implementation used at runtime. It does not choose an implementation when the program runs. So overriding is native inherited dispatch, while overloading needs an explicit Python technique matched to the actual requirement.

sections.title: One name can hold only the current class-body value
sections.content:
Executing a class body creates names much like executing other Python code. Each `def` creates a function and assigns it to its name. Repeating the name performs another assignment, so the class finally contains only the last function under that key. Parameter annotations do not alter this runtime rule.

Overriding happens at a different level. The base and subclass each keep their own method attribute. Lookup begins from the receiver's actual class, which makes the subclass method take precedence while the base implementation remains reachable through `super()`.

Several tools solve situations casually called overloading. Defaults and keyword-only arguments express small variations; distinct names communicate genuinely different operations; single dispatch chooses by the first argument's runtime type; static overload declarations describe type relationships for tooling. Choosing deliberately avoids pretending Python uses signature dispatch when it does not.

sections.title: The mechanisms are not interchangeable
sections.content:
| Mechanism | Selects at runtime? | Main purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Overriding | Yes, through class MRO | Specialize inherited behaviour |
| Default arguments | One implementation handles variations | Optional inputs |
| `singledispatchmethod` | Yes, primarily by first argument type | Type-directed dispatch |
| `typing.overload` | No | Describe related signatures to static checkers |
| Repeated same-name `def` | No overload created | Last definition replaces earlier ones |
